name: Waling
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: All nouns have a simple citation form and nouns in an unmarked (absolutive) position appear in that citation form. Pure, native Bantawa nouns comply with the phonological rules for syllable forms and syllabification. Except when the noun is a derivation of a verb or other category, the rather weak word stress falls on the first syllable. In case of derivations, the word stress falls on the root of the derivation. [p. 140:] The first syllable of infinitives bears the weak word stress, realised in higher pitch and greater amplitude. ... Since Bantawa is not a tone language in general, we can assign L as the default tone to all syllables

Utrecht: LOT (Leiden University PhD). Describes the Hatuva (Bhojpur) = Hatuwali dialect of Bantawa, which per ISO 639-3 CR 2018-005 is what the Waling/Walahang clan speaks.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Weak word stress on the first syllable of underived nouns and of infinitives; in derived words stress sits on the root of the derivation (so it is non-initial after prefixes such as the active-participle ka-). This is a Bantawa statement; no source states anything about stress under the name Waling.
new_statements.exceptions: Derived nouns/verbs (stress on the root, not the first syllable). A marginal high tone on the root syllable of t- and s-conjugation verb stems before consonants (p. 140, 'subphonemic residue'; p. 54 calls it a phonemic tone contrast limited to certain dialects); otherwise no lexical or grammatical tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: citation forms of nouns (absolutive) and infinitives; pitch/amplitude description of infinitives on p. 140. Variety: Hatuva-area Bantawa (Bhojpur), i.e. bant1281, not a corpus labelled Waling. The only Waling-labelled primary data (Hodgson 1857 wordlist; Grierson 1909 notes pp. 357-358) are explicitly silent: 'The materials are not sufficient for describing the phonetic system of the various dialects' (Grierson 1909: 340).
new_statements.identity_note: 'Waling' is not a separately described language. Hodgson 1857 already listed Waling as a Bontawa (= Bantawa) sept, Grierson 1909: 357 treats it as 'the Waling sept of the Bontawa Khambus', and ISO 639-3 CR 2018-005 (N. M. Rai, SIL, after a 2016 survey in Khairang, Bhojpur) reports that Waling/Walahang is a Bantawa clan name whose members speak the Hatuwali (Southern) dialect of Bantawa [bap] = bant1281, with no memory of a separate language; the RA nonetheless rejected the merge (2019-01-25), and Glottolog 5.3 keeps wali1261 as an extinct language (Ethnologue: 'Shifted to Bantawa [bap] in the late 1800s'). Doornenbal 2009 describes exactly the Hatuva-area Bantawa (Khairang is in his Hatuva thum list, p. 9), so the quoted stress statement is for bant1281, which is already in the catalog (set by morphology). Recommend recording wali1261 as an alias/clan lect of bant1281 rather than as a new entry.

In case of derivations, the word stress falls on the root of the derivation'; p. 140 'The first syllable of infinitives bears the weak word stress, realised in higher pitch and greater amplitude'; tone marginal (high tone on t-/s-conjugation root syllables), 'Bantawa is not a tone language in general'. Already in the catalog under bant1281 (set by morphology). Waling itself is mentioned only as a personal name in the glossary (waliŋhaŋ).

sources.note: Nothing on phonology. Identity only: 'Waling is a sept/clan within the ethnic group of Bantawa. The Waling people speak Bantawa language as their mother tongue' (p. 2); after a 2016 survey in the 'Waling village' Khairang, Bhojpur, 'They claimed no knowledge of a separate/independent Waling language, either now or in the past' (p. 4); 'The people from the Walahang (Waling) sept/clan speak the Hatuwali (Southern) dialect of Bantawa' (p. 5). States that only Hodgson 1857 and Grierson 1909 ever used 'Waling' as a language name.

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. (ed; Tibeto-Burman part by Sten Konow). 1909. Linguistic Survey of India, vol. III part I: Tibeto-Burman family. Calcutta: Office of the Superintendent of Government Printing. 'Minor Khambu dialects' p. 340 (341 in some scans), comparative vocabulary pp. 341-342, 'Waling' pp. 357-358.

sources.note: Explicitly silent. Intro to the minor Khambu dialects (which include Waling): 'The materials are not sufficient for describing the phonetic system of the various dialects. The so-called abrupt tone occurs in all of them. It has been indicated by means of an ' after the syllable so pronounced; thus, Balali pik', cow.' (p. 340). The Waling note (pp. 357-358) covers nouns, genitive, pronouns and verb fragments from Hodgson's list only; no phonetics. Khambu (Darjeeling) section: 'We have no information about the use of tones and accent.'

sources.citation: Hodgson, Brian Houghton. 1857. Comparative vocabulary of the several languages (dialects) of the celebrated people called Kirantis. Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal 26: 333-371 (Waling = item 5 of the Kiranti list, marked 'Bontawa'; Lambichhong = 'Waling').
